stem_html:
Ceramicist Idris Fowler calls his glazes ______ rather than designed. He mixes the ash of whatever the kiln burned that week, keeps no record of proportions, and accepts that a colour he likes will not return.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "circumstantial"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "traditional", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "careless", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "experimental", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The unrepeatable is not the sloppy. One choice converts a deliberate practice into a failure.
  • “Rather than designed” is the axis. The answer must oppose intention, and experimenting is intentional.
  • Three details, one property.

Why A is right Each detail ties the glaze to the conditions of the week: the ash of whatever the kiln burned, no record of proportions, and a colour that will not return. A result produced by circumstances rather than by intention is circumstantial.

Why B is wrong Traditional would locate the practice in inherited method, and the passage describes a practice that cannot be repeated even by Fowler himself.

Why C is wrong Careless implies he is failing at something he is trying to do. He accepts the irreproducibility, which makes it a choice rather than a lapse.

Why D is wrong Experimental suggests a search for a result. Fowler is not testing toward anything; he takes what the week supplies.

stem_html:
The new evidence does not overturn Marchetti's chronology so much as ______ it: every date she proposed still stands, and each now rests on two independent measurements instead of one.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"qualify","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"corroborate"},{"letter":"C","content":"complicate","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"supersede","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Not so much X as Y” needs Y to oppose X. One choice is a synonym for X.
  • “Every date still stands” rules out any weakening word.
  • Two measurements instead of one is the whole evidence, and it points one way.

Why A is wrong Qualify would mean the chronology now holds with reservations, but the passage says every date still stands without exception.

Why B is right The colon reports that every date she proposed still stands and now rests on two independent measurements. Additional independent support is corroboration.

Why C is wrong Complicate would mean the picture got harder, and the sentence describes it getting firmer.

Why D is wrong Supersede is a synonym for the verb the sentence contrasts the blank with. If the evidence superseded the chronology it would be overturning it.

stem_html:
Grief, the novel suggests, is ______ rather than continuous. The narrator manages three ordinary weeks and then loses an afternoon to a bus timetable her mother once annotated, and the chapters are arranged so that the reader is ambushed in the same way.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"private","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"unbearable","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"intermittent"},{"letter":"D","content":"diminishing","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The contrast word fixes the category. “Continuous” asks for a word about pattern, not about degree.
  • A trend where the passage shows an alternation.
  • The strongest word is not the most precise one.

Why A is wrong Private concerns who witnesses the grief. The chapters are arranged to ambush the reader, which if anything makes it shared.

Why B is wrong Unbearable is an intensity, not a pattern, and it does not contrast with “continuous.”

Why C is right The evidence is a pattern of gaps and returns: the narrator “manages three ordinary weeks and then loses an afternoon” to an annotated timetable. Something that stops and starts is intermittent, which is what “rather than continuous” calls for.

Why D is wrong Diminishing describes a trend over time, and the passage describes an alternation with no direction. The afternoon comes after the ordinary weeks.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2022 article about antibiotic discovery.

Screening soil bacteria for antibiotics has produced almost nothing new since 1987, and the standard reading is that the accessible chemistry has been exhausted. Nwachukwu's group re-screened the same soil collections but grew each strain beside a competitor rather than alone, and recovered eleven compounds no earlier screen had seen. The compounds are not new to the bacteria; they are made only when a rival is present, and a strain cultured by itself never produces them.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It argues that soil bacteria are a more promising source of antibiotics than marine bacteria.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"It explains why bacteria produce antibiotic compounds when competitors are present.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"C","content":"It reports the discovery of eleven bacterial species previously unknown to science.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"It reports a change in method that recovered compounds the standard approach could not detect, undercutting the usual explanation for a shortage."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Compounds against species. The number attaches to the wrong noun in one choice.
  • A finding read as an explanation.
  • The point is about the method, and the method is the one thing the passage changes.

Why A is wrong Marine bacteria are never mentioned, so no comparison of sources is made.

Why B is wrong That the compounds are made only when a rival is present is the finding, and the passage offers no explanation of why bacteria behave that way.

Why C is wrong Eleven compounds, not eleven species, and the strains came from collections already held. The passage says the compounds are not new to the bacteria.

Why D is right The passage states the standard reading, changes one variable in the method, and reports the result: eleven compounds no earlier screen had seen, made only when a rival is present. The shortage was a limit of the assay, not of the chemistry.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from Willa Cather's 1918 novel My Antonia.

I sat down in the middle of the garden, where snakes could scarcely approach unseen, and leaned my back against a warm yellow pumpkin. There were some ground-cherry bushes growing along the furrows, full of fruit. I turned back the papery triangular sheaths that protected the berries and ate a few. All about me giant grasshoppers, twice as big as any I had ever seen, were doing acrobatic feats among the dried vines. I kept as still as I could. Nothing happened. I did not expect anything to happen.

Which choice best describes the function of the final three sentences in the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "They convert a passage of close observation into a statement of the narrator's contentment with inactivity."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "They reveal that the narrator is afraid of the snakes mentioned in the first sentence.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "They explain why the narrator has come to the garden.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "They introduce a change in the setting that the rest of the passage develops.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Nothing happened” sounds like disappointment until the next sentence redefines it.
  • The snakes are dealt with in the first sentence and never return.
  • Final sentences cannot introduce what follows.

Why A is right The passage catalogues what is around the narrator, then turns inward: I kept as still as I could, nothing happened, and the last sentence makes the absence of event welcome rather than disappointing.

Why B is wrong The snakes appear once, and the narrator's choice of seat handles them practically. Nothing in the last three sentences returns to fear.

Why C is wrong No reason for the visit is given anywhere in the passage.

Why D is wrong The setting does not change, and these are the final sentences, so nothing follows for them to introduce.

Text 1

Remote work reduces productivity. Firms that went fully remote in 2020 shipped fewer products in the two years that followed than comparable firms that returned to offices, and the gap widened over time.

Text 2

Ahmadi separates two things the shipping figures run together. Output per engineer-hour was slightly higher at the remote firms throughout. What fell was the number of engineer-hours: the remote firms lost senior staff to competitors at nearly twice the rate, and each departure took months to replace.

Based on the texts, how would Ahmadi (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"By showing that senior staff at the remote firms were less productive than junior staff.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"By arguing that the shortfall reflects a loss of staff rather than a decline in how productively people worked."},{"letter":"C","content":"By denying that the remote firms shipped fewer products.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"By agreeing that remote work reduces productivity and adding that it also increases turnover.","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A total falling for two possible reasons. The answer has to name which.
  • Per-hour output rose, which is the sentence that rules out the productivity reading.
  • Accepting the headline while rejecting the interpretation.

Why A is wrong No comparison between senior and junior productivity appears. Seniority matters in Text 2 only because senior staff left.

Why B is right Ahmadi accepts the shipping gap and decomposes it: output per engineer-hour was slightly higher at the remote firms, and what fell was the number of engineer-hours. The cause is headcount, not productivity.

Why C is wrong She does not dispute the shipping figures; she separates two things they run together.

Why D is wrong She reports higher output per hour, so agreeing that productivity fell contradicts her central measurement.

stem_html:
Ornithologist Bea Okpara proposed that city robins sing at night because daytime traffic noise masks their songs, not because street lighting disturbs their sleep.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okpara's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Robins exposed to artificial light in a laboratory slept less than robins kept in darkness.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"Daytime traffic noise in the city centre was loud enough to mask robin song at a distance of twenty metres.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"Robins in brightly lit but quiet suburbs sang no more at night than rural robins, while robins in dark but noisy industrial districts sang at night as much as city-centre robins."},{"letter":"D","content":"Robins in the city centre, which is both brightly lit and noisy, sang at night far more than rural robins.","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two factors that travel together. The evidence has to pull them apart.
  • The rival's evidence offered as support.
  • Possible mechanism against operative mechanism.

Why A is wrong This supports the explanation Okpara rejects, and it is about sleep rather than about singing.

Why B is wrong That noise can mask song establishes the mechanism is possible without showing it is the one operating. It leaves light untested.

Why C is right Light and noise occur together in the city, so only a comparison that separates them can decide whether robins sing at night “because daytime traffic noise masks their songs, not because street lighting disturbs their sleep”. Bright and quiet gives no night singing; dark and noisy gives plenty.

Why D is wrong The city centre has both factors at once, so this cannot say which is responsible. It restates the phenomenon.

stem_html:
A curator argues that a set of undated bronzes was cast by one workshop over a short period rather than accumulated over generations, on the grounds that a single workshop working quickly would show a consistent alloy recipe while an accumulation would not.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the curator's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"All fourteen bronzes depict subjects drawn from the same body of myth.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"B","content":"The lead isotopes in the bronzes match ore from a single mine that was worked for four centuries.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"Two of the fourteen bronzes show casting flaws of the same unusual kind.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"The tin content of all fourteen bronzes falls within a range of half a percentage point, whereas bronzes from a securely dated multigenerational collection vary by six points."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A number needs a comparison. Half a percentage point means nothing without the six.
  • Same source, any duration.
  • Two items out of fourteen is not a property of the set.

Why A is wrong Shared subject matter says something about iconography and nothing about when or where the metal was worked. Workshops copy subjects for centuries.

Why B is wrong A single source mine worked for four centuries is consistent with a short period and equally consistent with accumulation, so it cannot separate them.

Why C is wrong Two out of fourteen is suggestive and falls short of the consistency the argument rests on, and shared flaws can also arise from shared technique across generations.

Why D is right The curator's stated test is that “a single workshop working quickly would show a consistent alloy recipe while an accumulation would not”, and this supplies it with a comparison that makes the number meaningful: half a point across the set against six points in a collection known to have accumulated.

stem_html:
A study measured how long four groups of participants persisted at an unsolvable puzzle. Each group was told a different thing beforehand about how others had done. The researchers concluded that persistence rose with the perceived difficulty of the task but levelled off once the task was described as nearly impossible.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Persistence rose by about 52 seconds from easy to moderate and by about 66 from moderate to hard, but by only about 7 from hard to nearly impossible."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Participants told the task was nearly impossible persisted longest.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Participants told the task was easy persisted for less than half as long as those told it was hard.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Persistence increased across all four framings.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The plateau lives in one interval. Any description that omits it cannot support the conclusion.
  • The largest bar is not the finding.
  • “Increased throughout” contradicts “levelled off.”

Why A is right The conclusion is that “persistence rose with the perceived difficulty of the task but levelled off”, so it needs a rise and a plateau, and only this choice gives both: two large steps of roughly 52 and 66 seconds, then a step of about 7.

Why B is wrong The tallest bar is consistent with a plateau and with a continuing rise, so it cannot distinguish them.

Why C is wrong A true comparison that skips the interval where the levelling off happens.

Why D is wrong “Increased across all four” describes a continuing rise, which is what the second half of the conclusion denies.

stem_html: In her collection Slack Water, the poet Fen Adeyinka writes about labour in a way that keeps the worker's body present while the product of the work disappears from view. Which quotation from a fictional poem would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"“A thousand doors, a thousand hinges, and the sound / of the shop was the sound of hinges being set.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"“Forty years of her wrists, and not one of the thousand doors / she hung is named in any ledger I can find.”"},{"letter":"C","content":"“The doors she hung are standing yet, and every one / swings true, and no one knows her name.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"“She worked until her wrists gave out, and then / she sat, and the shop went on without her.”","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two conditions, and each wrong choice satisfies one.
  • Name against product. An unrecognised worker is not the same as an invisible object.
  • Implied bodies are not present ones.

Why A is wrong This is the product in abundance and the body only implied. Hinges and sound fill the lines; no wrists, arms or hands appear.

Why B is right The body is foregrounded — forty years of her wrists — and the claim asks that it stay present “while the product of the work disappears from view”: the doors exist and are in no ledger the speaker can find. Both halves of the claim are present.

Why C is wrong The doors are emphatically visible here, standing and swinging true. What disappears is her name, which is recognition rather than the product.

Why D is wrong The wrists are present and nothing is said about the product at all. The shop going on is about her absence, not about the work's visibility.

The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about language documentation.

A dictionary is the standard product of language documentation, and a language is often counted as documented once one exists. Working with speakers of a Papuan language, Bakhtiari found that the dictionary compiled in 1994 recorded 4,200 words and no verb morphology, because the elicitation sessions had been conducted in Tok Pisin and the fieldworker had asked for nouns. The gap is not a matter of degree, she argues: a speaker with the dictionary and nothing else could name every object in the room and could not form a sentence.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Elicitation sessions should not be conducted through a contact language.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"Papuan languages are more morphologically complex than the languages of surrounding regions.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"A dictionary can leave a language undocumented in the respects that matter most, so its existence is a poor test of documentation."},{"letter":"D","content":"The 1994 dictionary of a Papuan language recorded 4,200 words.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Cause of the defect against the defect itself.
  • The number is the most concrete thing on the page and it is evidence.
  • “Not a matter of degree” is the phrase that makes this an argument about the test.

Why A is wrong Tok Pisin explains how the gap arose and is one clause of one sentence. The argument is about what the dictionary fails to be, not about method reform.

Why B is wrong No comparison with other regions appears anywhere.

Why C is right The passage names the standard test, shows what it misses, and states the consequence: a speaker with the dictionary and nothing else could name every object in the room and could not form a sentence.

Why D is wrong The word count is the evidence, given in the middle of the sentence that makes the argument.

The following text is adapted from a 2020 article about the Chicago Defender.

The Defender is remembered for its editorials urging Black southerners northward, and historians have cited them as a cause of the Great Migration. Reading the paper's distribution records, Boateng finds that in the Mississippi Delta the paper circulated hand to hand through Pullman porters, and that a single copy was read aloud to gatherings of thirty or more. The editorials mattered, she argues, but so did the fact that the paper arrived as an event rather than as a private object.

According to the text, what does Boateng's reading of the distribution records indicate?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The editorials had less influence than historians have claimed.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"Pullman porters wrote much of the paper's editorial content.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"Most readers in the Mississippi Delta owned their own copies.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"How the paper was circulated and read contributed to its influence alongside what it argued."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “But so did” adds; it does not subtract.
  • Carrying against writing.
  • One copy, thirty listeners is the detail one choice reverses.

Why A is wrong She says the editorials mattered. Adding a second factor is not demoting the first.

Why B is wrong The porters carried the paper. Nothing suggests they wrote for it.

Why C is wrong A single copy was read aloud to gatherings of thirty or more, which is the opposite of individual ownership.

Why D is right Her conclusion keeps both factors: the editorials mattered, but so did the fact that the paper arrived as an event rather than as a private object.

stem_html:
An alloy becomes brittle below a transition temperature that depends on its grain size. A manufacturer tested two batches from the same melt. Batch X, cooled slowly, has coarse grains and a transition temperature of 5 degrees Celsius; batch Y, quenched, has fine grains and a transition temperature of -40. Both batches have the same composition and were tested on the same rig. It follows that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "grain size, and not composition, accounts for the difference in transition temperature between the batches."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "quenching lowers the transition temperature of every alloy.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "batch X is stronger than batch Y at room temperature.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the transition temperature cannot be predicted from a batch's cooling rate.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Same melt, same rig. Those two clauses are what license the inference.
  • Generalising from one alloy.
  • A second property smuggled in. Brittle is not weak.

Why A is right The two batches come from the same melt and were tested on the same rig, so composition and method are held constant. Grain size is the one thing that differs, and it is what the transition temperature depends on.

Why B is wrong One alloy cannot establish a claim about every alloy. The passage gives a mechanism through grain size, not a universal rule about quenching.

Why C is wrong Strength at room temperature is a different property, and neither batch's strength is measured. Brittleness below a transition temperature says nothing about behaviour above it.

Why D is wrong The passage shows the opposite: the batch cooled slowly and the batch quenched differ predictably, through grain size.

stem_html:
A museum introduced a pay-what-you-wish evening. Attendance on those evenings tripled, and total admissions revenue for the evenings rose by 8 percent. The museum's shop takings on those evenings, however, fell by a fifth per visitor while rising in total. Since prices in the shop were unchanged, this suggests that the evenings ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"should be extended to every evening of the week.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"drew visitors who spend less on average than the museum's usual evening audience."},{"letter":"C","content":"reduced the museum's total income.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"attracted visitors who were less interested in the collection.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Per visitor against in total. The two move in opposite directions and both are stated.
  • Inferring motive from spending.
  • From a finding to a policy.

Why A is wrong A recommendation does not follow from these figures, which say nothing about costs or about what would happen at other times.

Why B is right Takings “fell by a fifth per visitor while rising in total”, and since prices in the shop were unchanged, the average visitor on those evenings spends less than the average visitor before. The total rose only because there were three times as many of them.

Why C is wrong Both admissions revenue and total shop takings rose. Nothing in the passage shows income falling.

Why D is wrong Interest in the collection is not measured. Spending less in a shop is consistent with any level of interest, and with a smaller budget.

The expedition carried one instrument that had never been taken above 6,000 metres ______ magnetometer built for a submarine and adapted in the field.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":", it was a","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":"a","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"C","content":": a"},{"letter":"D","content":"; a","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “One instrument” is a promise.
  • A comma before a full clause is a splice, however naturally the second half follows the first.
  • A noun phrase is not a clause.

Why C is right The first clause is complete and names an instrument without identifying it; a colon after an independent clause introduces the identification.

Why D is wrong A semicolon joins independent clauses, and what follows is a noun phrase.

Since the ice core was drilled in a single season and stored at a constant temperature ______ layers can be counted without correcting for post-depositional flow.

The two methods agree on the age of the eruption ______ disagree by four centuries on the age of the flow beneath it, and nobody has explained why.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":": they","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"; they"},{"letter":"C","content":", they","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"D","content":"they","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"}]

Each of the twenty-three settlements identified in the survey ______ within a day's walk of a perennial spring.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"have lain","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":"were lying","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"lies"},{"letter":"D","content":"lie","trap":"distant-antecedent"}]

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Which” selects one, so the possessive must be singular.
  • Apostrophe placement is the whole difference between two of the choices.
  • A pronoun cannot follow “which” here at all.

Why A is wrong “Sides'” is the plural possessive and has the same problem as “their,” with the added defect that “which” then has nothing singular to select.

Why B is right “Which” is asking the jury to choose between two parties, so the noun after it has to name a single one of them. “Side's” is the singular possessive that does so.

Why C is wrong “Their” is plural and would ask which account belonging to both parties, which is not a choice at all.

Why D is wrong “Its” is singular but its referent is undetermined, and “which its account” is not a possible English phrase.

Vertical farms are promoted as a way to cut the emissions of food transport, and the distance from a warehouse farm to a city supermarket is indeed a few kilometres rather than a few thousand. ______ transport accounts for under 6 percent of the emissions of most vegetables, while the lighting a vertical farm needs can exceed the whole footprint of a field crop.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Likewise,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"That is,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"However,"},{"letter":"D","content":"Accordingly,","trap":"transition-reversal"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Indeed” in the first sentence is a concession, which sets up a reversal.
  • Consequence where there is contradiction.
  • New evidence is not a restatement.

Why A is wrong “Likewise” asserts agreement, and the sentences disagree.

Why B is wrong “That is” announces a restatement, and the second sentence introduces new figures that cut the other way.

Why C is right The second sentence undercuts the case the first concedes, so the transition marks the turn.

Why D is wrong “Accordingly” would make the emissions figures a consequence of the short distance, which reverses the logic.

The manuscript was copied twice in the twelfth century, and both copies survive. The original does not. ______ everything known about the text comes from comparing two documents that were themselves copied by hand.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Nonetheless,","trap":"transition-reversal"},{"letter":"B","content":"For example,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"Meanwhile,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"Consequently,"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A missing original and a consequence.
  • Concession where there is entailment.
  • Result against instance.

Why A is wrong “Nonetheless” would set the third sentence against the second, but it follows from it.

Why B is wrong The dependence on copies is not an example of the original's loss; it is what the loss produces.

Why C is wrong “Meanwhile” marks simultaneity, and no second timeline is running.

Why D is right The loss of the original is the reason scholarship depends on the two copies, so the transition marks a consequence.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Sargasso Sea has no coasts; it is bounded by ocean currents.
  • European and American eels both spawn there and nowhere else.
  • Larvae drift on currents for up to three years before reaching rivers.
  • Tesfaye tagged 26 adult eels and tracked them from Europe.
  • All 26 tags stopped transmitting before the Sargasso Sea was reached.

The student wants to emphasize a limitation of Tesfaye's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Although Tesfaye tagged 26 adult eels and tracked them from Europe, every tag stopped transmitting before the Sargasso Sea was reached."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Tesfaye tagged 26 adult eels and tracked them on their migration from Europe.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "European and American eels spawn in the Sargasso Sea and nowhere else, and their larvae drift for up to three years before reaching rivers.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The Sargasso Sea has no coasts, which makes it difficult to study.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A limitation needs the ambition and the shortfall together.
  • Background offered as a limitation.
  • “Although” is what makes one sentence do the work of two.

Why A is right A limitation is a gap between what a study set out to show and what it reached, and only this choice puts both sides in one sentence: 26 tagged eels, and no tag surviving to the destination.

Why B is wrong This is the study without its shortfall, which is the half the goal excludes.

Why C is wrong This is background about eels and contains nothing about Tesfaye's study.

Why D is wrong The absence of coasts is a fact about the sea, and the difficulty it creates is the student's inference rather than a limitation of this study.
